analysis.one_liner: Permanently extends business tax breaks and cuts the top corporate tax rate to 30%.
analysis.headline: The bill, a corporate tax cut introduced by Rep. Jim Gerlach with one Democratic cosponsor, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in May 2011 and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make permanent the federal research tax credit and raise its alternative credit rate to 20%, make permanent higher small-business expensing limits, and cut the top corporate income tax rate from 35% to 30%, including for personal service corporations. It contains no revenue offsets, so the tax cuts would add to the federal deficit unless paid for elsewhere. It also directs two government studies, one on workplace health clinics and one on keeping rural college graduates in their home regions.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and their shareholders gain the most from the permanent cut in the top corporate rate from 35% to 30%. Research-intensive companies gain from a permanent, larger research credit. Small and mid-sized businesses gain from making permanent the ability to deduct up to $250,000 in equipment purchases immediately rather than over time. Personal service corporations get the same 30% top rate.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporations, research firms, and business owners

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the top corporate marginal tax rate from 35% to 30% for all corporations, including personal service corporations [S2] [S3].
Makes the research tax credit permanent (it otherwise required periodic renewal) and raises the alternative simplified credit rate from 14% to 20% [S2] [S3].
Makes permanent the increased Section 179 expensing allowance, letting businesses deduct up to $250,000 of equipment purchases in the year bought [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: With no offsets in the bill, the cost lands on the federal Treasury, meaning taxpayers generally through higher future deficits or debt. If the cuts were ever paid for instead, the cost would fall on whatever programs or taxpayers were tapped to offset them. The bill text includes no such pay-fors.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no revenue offsets: making the research credit permanent, expanding expensing, and cutting the corporate rate all reduce federal revenue, adding to deficits unless Congress cuts spending or raises taxes elsewhere [S2] [S3].
Permanent corporate tax cuts flow to shareholders, who are disproportionately higher-income households, and the bill gives no corresponding relief to wage earners [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The expensing provision for small businesses is a modest, widely used benefit, but the bill's largest provisions — the permanent corporate rate cut and permanent research credit — are large revenue giveaways with no pay-fors, meaning the cost would eventually be borne by taxpayers through deficits or offsets elsewhere. As written, the concentrated gains outweigh any broad public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Gerlach introduced the bill on May 5, 2011, with Rep. Larry Kissell as its sole cosponsor [S3] [S4].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the same day; the committee never reported it or scheduled action, and no vote ever took place [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No industry gained anything, since the bill never moved. Taxpayers in general are marginally better off because the unoffset corporate rate cut and permanent research credit never became law, leaving federal revenue untouched.

for.name: Rep. Jim Gerlach
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the top corporate rate to 30% and make the research credit and small-business expensing permanent.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill out, keeping it from any House vote.

sides.party_line_note: With one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, and no votes or committee action on record, there was no meaningful partisan test of the bill.

industries.note: The bill would cut their top tax rate from 35% to 30% permanently, a major revenue loss to the Treasury with no offset; the burden of covering that gap would eventually fall on taxpayers. The bill never advanced, so no gain materialized.

industries.industry: Research and development-intensive firms (pharma, tech, manufacturing)
industries.note: A permanent, larger research credit (20% alternative rate) would lock in an ongoing federal subsidy for firms that already claim it, paid for out of general revenue.
Permanent Section 179 expensing of up to $250,000 would let them deduct equipment immediately, aiding investment, though this too adds to deficits without a pay-for.
